entries.test: Public evidence of durable competitive advantages, switching costs, and customer retention among LLM companies offering substantially similar products would test whether product convergence precludes a moat.
entries.note: The claim is categorical but conditional on companies building substantially the same thing.

entries.test: OpenAI market-share trends since January 2024 and public evidence explaining customer switching would test whether a lack of competitive protection caused its decline.
entries.note: “That’s been catching” attributes OpenAI’s deterioration to the preceding claim about lacking a moat.

entries.test: Microsoft’s investment history, partnership terms, and adoption of alternatives through publication would establish its historical backing and whether its reliance on OpenAI was declining.
entries.note: “Backing away” has a plain reading in terms of investment, partnership commitments, and product reliance.
The central assertion evaluates the development as a strong negative signal without specifying an outcome it predicts.

entries.test: Zitron’s reported financial figures and previously published estimates of OpenAI’s spending and losses would establish whether the reported losses exceeded prior expectations.
entries.note: Marcus explicitly adopts the report’s implication in his own voice; the embedded financial quotation remains Zitron’s.

entries.test: Successive annual financial disclosures and financing outcomes would show whether OpenAI sustained approximately eightfold annual loss growth or that trajectory ended.
entries.note: The financial trajectory is concrete, although “for very long” supplies no fixed deadline.
“Might succeed” explicitly presents a possibility, including its potential benefit to Kushner’s investment.
